en.help.entry.body: The dsh-graph board is maintained by a supervisor agent: it records goals and criteria, dispatches executions and collects results. In a new session, have one agent load the dsh-graph-supervisor skill (the full supervisor playbook) or the dsh-graph skill, then run graph_claim_supervisor() to take over (claim) - the agent then reads the current board state and the handoff document, and all further work starts there.
en.help.entry.copyFail: Copy failed - please select the text manually
en.help.entry.title: Step 1: pick a supervisor agent first
en.help.faq.a1: It gives agents a "goal board" way of working: you write down what to achieve and how it will be judged, dispatch the work, then review the outcome.
en.help.faq.a2: A goal is what to achieve; criteria define what counts as achieved (written before work starts); cards collect the context and conclusions produced along the way.
en.help.faq.a3: Sections (version / standalone goal / backlog) show scheduling; statuses show the stage a goal is in, from draft and planning through in progress to awaiting review, delivered or postponed.
en.help.faq.a4: It may, within the scope defined by the goal and its criteria; when isolation is needed the work happens in a separate git worktree and your main working copy stays untouched.
en.help.faq.a5: Starting work, accepting a result and releasing a version are human gates: the agent can only ask, and you decide whether it passes.
en.help.faq.a6: Board data lives in the .dsh-graph directory of the current workspace, so it travels with that workspace; a different workspace is a different board.
en.help.faq.a7: Yes. The "Modules" tab of the board settings has five switches — tags, memory, shared cards, automation prompts and attachments — stored per workspace in project.yaml. Turning a module off really removes the matching graph_* tools and the prompt sections delivered to agents (it does not merely hide buttons).

en.help.faq.q2: How do goals, criteria and cards differ?

en.help.mod.board.how: Open it from the Kanban tab in the DSH Web right sidebar; the top toolbar holds refresh, tag filter, Memory, Help, Project knowledge base and Kanban settings, and on narrow widths those entries collapse into the overflow menu.
en.help.mod.board.ops: Click a card to open the goal detail; create goals from a lane header; when the view contains status=review goals, the Confirm column header shows a Batch accept button (it accepts one by one without force, with the same semantics as accepting a single card).
en.help.mod.board.title: Board
en.help.mod.board.what: The main view after opening the plugin: goals are grouped into versions / standalone / backlog and rendered as cards that show status, criteria and the latest execution at a glance.
en.help.mod.cards.how: Add and read cards in the Information Collection section of the goal detail; the Project knowledge base entry in the top toolbar opens the shared-entries panel.
en.help.mod.cards.ops: Create, fill, review and delete cards; convert an owned card into a shared card and back; attach and detach shared cards (goal owner or supervisor only); an attachment still referenced by a card cannot be deleted; a backlog goal cannot own cards, schedule it first.
en.help.mod.cards.title: Context cards and the project knowledge base
en.help.mod.cards.what: Cards hold the context and conclusions collected while working (body text plus optional @att/<name> attachment references); shared cards live in the project knowledge base and one card can be attached to several goals to reuse its context.
en.help.mod.goal.how: Create it from the lane header; click a card for the goal detail with Goal Description, Quality Criteria, Information Collection and recent activity.
en.help.mod.goal.ops: Write the criteria before working (registering criteria snapshots the rule-library version); transition status (entering blocked requires a reason); schedule into a version / standalone / backlog; archive, postpone, rename, tag and relate goals.
en.help.mod.goal.title: Goals
en.help.mod.goal.what: A goal is what must be achieved: each one carries a status, quality criteria, description, latest directive, tags and relations. Status runs draft, planning, collecting, ready, in_progress, review, delivered, plus blocked.
en.help.mod.intro: The nine chapters below cover the modules of the board; each has three lines: what it is, how to use it (UI location or tool name) and key operations.
en.help.mod.lane.how: The arrow left of a lane title collapses or expands it; a collapsed lane shows a single row with its goal count, and the collapsed state is stored per workspace.
en.help.mod.lane.ops: Drag cards between stages or lanes (the state machine constrains this: a backlog card may only go to the Describe column of a version, a blocked goal may only be released back to its original status, and an illegal move is rejected with a reason); create a goal for that version straight from the lane header.
en.help.mod.lane.title: Lanes
en.help.mod.lane.what: A lane is a horizontal group on the board: one per version plus Standalone and backlog; inside a lane, cards are laid out in stage columns - Describe, Collect, Execute, Confirm, Deliver, with a separate place for blocked goals.
en.help.mod.memory.how: The Memory entry in the top toolbar opens the Memory Management dialog, where entries can be searched, added, revised and removed.
en.help.mod.memory.ops: The supervisor distills conclusions into memory at key points (on_demand by default, so it costs no resident budget); removal requires the entry to be outdated or explicitly retracted by the owner; memory is stored per workspace under .dsh-graph.
en.help.mod.memory.title: Memory
en.help.mod.memory.what: Memory stores durable facts across sessions in two scopes: standing (injected into the resident prompt, with a hard cap) and on_demand (the default, retrieved only when needed).
en.help.mod.settings.how: Open it from the gear button at the top-right of the board (inside the overflow menu on narrow widths); a separate profile-level section in the DSH settings configures the subagent provider, model, reasoning effort, mode and prompt language.
en.help.mod.settings.ops: The Modules tab has five switches - tags, memory, shared cards, automation prompts and attachments - and turning one off really removes the matching tools and delivered prompt sections (the tab warns when the host does not support real trimming); Review & quality configures review.policy; Advanced holds the six supervisor automation switches and the subagent prompt override.
en.help.mod.settings.title: Common settings
en.help.mod.settings.what: The board settings dialog has five tabs: Model & execution / Review & quality / UI & refresh / Modules / Advanced; the configuration is stored per workspace in project.yaml.
en.help.mod.sidebar.how: Click the Kanban tab in the right sidebar; the tab title follows the UI language.
en.help.mod.sidebar.ops: One board per workspace (data lives in the .dsh-graph directory and travels with the workspace); when the host has no right-sidebar capability (minimal profile / older host) the plugin simply does not register the tab and reports no error.
en.help.mod.sidebar.title: Using the sidebar
en.help.mod.sidebar.what: The plugin registers a tab in the DSH Web right sidebar (titled Kanban, described as viewing and managing the goal board in this session) so the board sits next to the conversation.
en.help.mod.subagents.how: The supervisor dispatches execution with graph_start_attempt and an independent review with graph_start_review; every dispatch leaves an execution record on the goal whose status can be followed on the card.
en.help.mod.subagents.ops: Record the rework handoff constraints before dispatching again; unbind or abandon a lost subagent; the Model & execution tab configures the executor and model and carries the Agent Teams minimal-contract switch (off by default; only when it is on is the contract block injected into dispatch prompts).
en.help.mod.subagents.title: Subagents and agent teams
en.help.mod.subagents.what: Execution is dispatched to a subagent one attempt at a time (isolated into its own git worktree when needed) and its output is written to results-att-*.md; review can be dispatched separately to a read-only reviewer whose verdict is stored independently.
en.help.mod.title: Module chapters
en.help.mod.version.how: The Version management entry at the top-left of the board grid opens the version drawer: search by name or slug and use show all / active only / hide all to control lane visibility (that filter is stored locally and never changes version data).
en.help.mod.version.ops: Create, rename and delete versions (only empty versions can be deleted); use the Details link in the drawer for the version detail, which can also create and rename goals.
en.help.mod.version.title: Version management
en.help.mod.version.what: A version groups goals and is the release unit: each version owns one lane on the board and carries a slug, a status (active / released) and a goal count.

en.help.topic.core: That state machine is defined and organized by **dsh-graph core** (the core/ directory): transitions, criteria gates, dispatch and verdict rules all live there. This plugin is the **monitoring board view** of that division of labour. Once the core is stable, pleasant to use and simple enough, the same core can produce other views - a dsh TUI, or a pi-ai plugin, for instance.
en.help.topic.definition: > An article on mcp.so defining Graph Engineering puts it this way: "Graph Engineering means designing a multi-agent system as an explicit graph - nodes (agents or steps that each do exactly one thing), edges (sequential, conditional or parallel routing) and shared state - rather than relying on a single agent running one loop".
en.help.topic.definitionSource: The Chinese text above is quoted verbatim from the original; this English rendering is a translation. Source: mcp.so (the article on Graph Engineering).
en.help.topic.designCrossref: For the naming and the full "the board is only a view" explanation, see the opening chapter of the Getting started tab, "Why it is called dsh-graph: Graph Engineering and the board as a view"; this tab covers only how the design philosophy lands in practice - the two diagrams below are the fixed rendering of that division of labour in the **current version**.
en.help.topic.faqA: No. The board is only one **view** of that graph: it draws the current state of the state machine for you. The graph itself takes shape while you work together - its nodes are the agents or steps that each do one job, its edges are sequential, conditional or parallel routing, and its shared state is the goals, criteria, cards and memory. It changes with the task, so you never have to customize one fixed graph per task, and you do not have to watch it all the time. The real core is the whole-process constraint, the division of labour between agents and the layered approval control; the board makes all of that visible and keeps an entry point ready for you to cut in. Graph customization will open up in later versions.
en.help.topic.kanbanIsView: So one question is worth asking first: **do you really need to see this graph all the time? Do you need many different graphs? Do you need to customize one graph per task?** The board is only one view of that graph. The real core is three things: the constraint on the AI's whole process, the division of labour between agents, and the layered approval control that runs from user to supervisor to worker.
en.help.topic.lifecycle: A piece of work moves along one lifecycle chain: new request → define goal and criteria → collect → implement → review → verdict → deliver. It has two loops: **rework** goes from verdict back to implement, and **branching out a new goal** splits a fresh goal chain off the step that needs to be broken up, each progressing on its own.
en.help.topic.naming: The name dsh-graph comes from **Graph Engineering**: designing a multi-agent system as an explicit **graph**, instead of relying on a single agent running one loop.
en.help.topic.programmable: What Graph Engineering adds is making the organization of agents **programmable**. But that programming is **not** about specifying nodes and edges in a DSL - it is closer to a software engineering practice: how humans and AIs, and agents and agents, work together. Describing it clearly is enough; tell yourself and the agent in natural language and the "programming" is done.
en.help.topic.roadmap: The roadmap, stated honestly: **graph customization will open up in later versions** (graph semantics tuning, visual customization and so on), while **the current version focuses on process visualization plus the task state machine**. The diagrams in this dialog are the fixed ones shipped with the package and cannot be adjusted yet.
en.help.topic.roles: Inside that state machine the roles are not pre-assigned positions; they **emerge naturally**: the supervisor records goals and criteria and dispatches and rules on them, workers (subagents) do the actual work, reviewers check results independently, definers turn a request into a clear goal, collectors gather the context first, and the user (you) holds the human gates. Only two things constrain them: the **supervisor guide** (the dsh-graph-supervisor skill) and the **goal state machine** itself - what may happen when is decided by the state and the guide, not by someone handing out assignments mid-conversation.
en.help.topic.solves: So what does the board solve here? Mainly two things. First, **making the whole process visible**: at a glance you can tell what the agents are doing, how the task was broken up, how stages advance, where it fell back or was reworked, and where new requirements and new goals branched off. Second, **letting you cut in at any time**: you can step into any detail, or discuss direction, method, goal changes and version plans with the supervisor agent whenever you like - and those discussions are recorded on the goal instead of being scattered across the conversation.
en.help.topic.stateMachine: Concretely, this plugin is a **task / goal state machine** maintenance system: for an AI it works like a **lightweight Jira + Confluence** (or, if you prefer, a ZenTao-style tracker) - I write down what to achieve and how it will be judged, the AI executes it, I decide the verdict, and both the process and the conclusions stay in one place.
en.help.topic.stateOfMind: **What matters is that you hold the graph in your head, not that the UI shows one fixed graph.** Once you and the AI are in flow, you can close your eyes and see it: who is doing what, how far along it is, where rework may be needed. It changes with the task, it is not fixed in advance, and you never have to customize one per task. That is also what the plugin name is there for - it reminds both me (the owner) and the AI that the board is only a view.
en.help.topic.title: Why it is called dsh-graph: Graph Engineering and the board as a view
en.help.usage.board: The board groups goal cards by version / standalone goal / backlog, and each card shows its status, criteria and latest execution.
en.help.usage.dispatch: Every dispatch leaves an execution record on the goal and writes its output to a result file; the same goal can be reworked as many times as needed.
en.help.usage.flow: Typical flow: create a goal and write its criteria → schedule it into a version or as a standalone goal → dispatch an execution (isolated in its own worktree when needed) → review the result.
en.help.usage.review: You decide the key gates: starting work, accepting or rejecting a result, and releasing a version. The engine never passes them for you.
en.help.usage.tabs: Other tabs in this dialog: prompt templates (the assets actually delivered to agents, read-only), tools (everything currently registered), FAQ, and graph design (two interactive diagrams).
en.help.usage.what: dsh-graph organizes work as a "goal board": goals, criteria, cards and executions are all managed on the board, and agents operate it through the graph_* tools.

en.settings.agentTeams: Agent Teams minimal contract (single-attempt fan-out + independent verification)
en.settings.agentTeamsHint: (Off by default; when on, the contract block is injected into the dispatch prompt — members are not attempts, an author self-report is not independent verification, trace under reviews/)
en.settings.automationDefaultScopeNotePrefi: Unset wording: the "Default: human" shown here is not an engine-resolved default; it is grounded in one of the four human gates in the Supervisor Guide — "
en.settings.automationDefaultScopeNoteSuffi: " — the action still sits inside that human gate and needs the owner's confirmation; when unset it keeps the existing guidance.
en.settings.automationHint: Affects the supervisor prompt: human asks the person in charge for confirmation, ai decides autonomously within the already authorized scope and leaves a trace, and unset keeps the existing guidance; it changes no tool permission and is not engine enforcement (it changes no existing gate such as start work, review, or release).
en.settings.automationWhat.integration_deci: Integration decision: whether a candidate implementation is merged, and whether a human must approve it first. human = the owner makes the merge call; ai = decide from verified evidence and record it in the event stream; unset = keep the existing guidance.
en.settings.automationWhat.memory_promotion: Memory promotion: turn this round experience into long-term memory, and whether it becomes standing. human = confirm promotion or standing status with the owner; ai = persist it by the tiering rules (on-demand by default; standing still obeys the hard cap); unset = keep the existing guidance.
en.settings.automationWhat.release: Release: who clears the version number, the release gate, and the release action. human = the owner must confirm the release action; ai = complete pre-release checks within the authorized scope and leave a trace, while the final release still obeys the existing gates; unset = keep the existing guidance.
en.settings.automationWhat.rework: Rework: when acceptance fails, send it back for another attempt or escalate to a human. human = confirm the criteria and constraints with the owner first; ai = register the rework handoff from verified failures and dispatch again; unset = keep the existing guidance.
en.settings.automationWhat.scope_planning: Scope planning: whether the goal is broken into execution scope and criteria before work starts. human = confirm scope and criteria with the owner first; ai = split it autonomously within the goal description and existing authorization, leaving a trace; unset = keep the existing guidance.
en.settings.automationWhat.skill_proposal: Skill proposal: whether a reusable workflow is written up as a skill proposal and submitted. human = confirm the content and submission with the owner; ai = draft the proposal and leave it pending approval; unset = keep the existing guidance.

en.settings.reviewCalibrationGuide: Aligned with the supervisor guide section "Review Strictness Calibration (Project-Specific)": the supervisor calibrates to the real project layout (confirming with the owner when needed), and graph_get_settings / graph_update_settings read and write the same project.yaml configuration.
en.settings.reviewClearTitle: Clear to an explicit empty list [] (different from unset)
en.settings.reviewConditionsHint: Supervisors set these three per project layout: top-level regions, contract paths, and non-product-code prefixes. The defaults are generic (not calibrated for this project); when unset the policy layer uses those defaults. Only an explicit entry is written to project.yaml.
en.settings.reviewConfigMalformed: The review configuration in project.yaml has unparsable fields (a whole-file syntax error, a review section that is not a mapping, or a list value that is invalid): those fields are treated as unusable (fail-closed), never refilled with the raw value, and cannot be edited. Fix project.yaml first; settings outside the review section can still be saved.
en.settings.reviewContractPathsHint: A change touching any contract path forces strict (a machine gate that an explicit auto/none cannot override). Unset uses the generic default (empty list; M1 does not trigger). An empty list [] is allowed.
en.settings.reviewEmptyForbidden: regions does not allow an explicit empty list (no evaluable region, fail-closed to strict). Register at least one region, or use "Reset to unset".
en.settings.reviewExplicitEmpty: Explicit empty list [] (submitted as empty, not unset)
en.settings.reviewIllegalEmpty: ⚠️ Invalid value: an explicit empty list is not allowed for regions (the write side rejects it and the engine escalates to strict via fail-closed) — add region entries, or click "Restore unset".
en.settings.reviewInvalidAbsolute: {field} entry #{index} "{item}" must not be an absolute path (including Windows drive letters)
en.settings.reviewInvalidDotDot: {field} entry #{index} "{item}" must not contain a .. path segment
en.settings.reviewInvalidEmpty: {field} entry #{index} must not be an empty string
en.settings.reviewInvalidReserved: {field} entry #{index} "{item}" must not use the internal reserved prefix invalid:
en.settings.reviewInvalidTrailingSlash: {field} entry #{index} "{item}" must not have a trailing slash
en.settings.reviewItemsPlaceholder: One entry per line (paths separated by /, no trailing slash)
en.settings.reviewMakeExplicitTitle: Copy the current default effective value into a writable draft (only on this explicit click)
en.settings.reviewMalformedField: This field has an invalid value and is treated as unusable (fail-closed)
en.settings.reviewNonProductPrefixesHint: Changes under these prefixes do not count as product-code lines (docs, generated files, dependencies). Unset uses the generic default. An empty list [] is allowed.
en.settings.reviewPolicyAuto: auto (automatic: fast-track eligible, gate hits still escalate to strict)
en.settings.reviewPolicyHint: When unset, the policy is derived from the goal type (patch/chore -> auto, otherwise -> strict). An explicit value overrides that derivation, but machine gates such as contract paths still force strict.
en.settings.reviewPolicyNone: none (no review: decision recorded only, delivery not blocked)
en.settings.reviewRegionsHint: Changes touching 3 or more regions escalate to strict; product code in unregistered regions also escalates to strict. An empty list is not allowed (no evaluable region; fail-closed to strict).
en.settings.reviewResetUnsetTitle: Submit null: remove the field from project.yaml and fall back to the generic default
